practice_questions.text: Define the term 'functionality' in the context of material selection.
practice_questions.marks: The suitability of a material for its intended purpose/application (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two aesthetic factors a designer might consider when selecting a material for a piece of furniture.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each valid aesthetic factor described, e.g.: Surface grain/texture of the wood gives a natural, warm appearance (1). Colour of the material matches the design style or interior decor (1). Surface finish such as gloss or matt affects visual appeal (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose FSC-certified timber over non-certified timber when manufacturing a bookcase.
practice_questions.marks: FSC certification ensures timber comes from sustainably managed forests (1) where trees are replanted to maintain the ecosystem (1). This appeals to environmentally conscious consumers and can improve brand reputation (1). Using certified timber also helps reduce deforestation and supports ethical forestry practices (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why cost is not always the most important factor when selecting a material for a product. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Detailed explanation with relevant examples. E.g. A children’s toy must prioritise safety over cost — ABS polymer is more expensive than some alternatives but it is non-toxic, impact resistant and has no sharp edges when moulded (up to 3). Environmental regulations may require recyclable materials even if they cost more (1). Ethical sourcing (Fairtrade cotton, FSC timber) adds cost but meets consumer expectations and legal requirements (1). A cheap material that fails in use damages brand reputation and costs more in returns/replacements (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited or no examples.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of recycled polymers versus virgin polymers for manufacturing food packaging. Consider functionality, cost and environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation covering all three factors with a supported conclusion. Recycled polymers reduce landfill waste and use less energy in production, lowering environmental impact. However, recycled polymers may have inconsistent properties and some are not food-safe without additional processing. Virgin polymers offer reliable, consistent quality and meet food safety regulations but contribute to fossil fuel depletion. Cost of recycled can be lower (reduced raw material) or higher (processing to food-grade). Conclusion weighing both sides.
Mid band (4-6): Covers at least two factors with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Limited points, mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: A company is designing a new range of outdoor garden chairs. Discuss the factors that would influence the selection of materials for this product. In your answer, consider at least four different selection factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion of 4+ factors with specific material examples and a clear conclusion. Factors include: functionality (weather resistance, UV stability, strength — e.g. treated softwood, HDPE, powder-coated aluminium), aesthetics (colour range, texture, modern vs traditional look), cost (budget vs premium range, bulk production savings), environmental impact (recyclable materials, FSC timber, recycled polymers), availability (standard stock forms, supplier reliability), ethical/social (safe manufacturing, fair labour). spelling/grammar: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar throughout.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion of 3–4 factors with examples.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant factors discussed, limited examples.
Lower band (1-3): Basic or superficial points. spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'shear force'.
practice_questions.marks: Two forces acting in opposite directions close together, causing a material to slide or tear apart (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between tension and compression.
practice_questions.marks: Tension is a pulling force that stretches a material (1). Compression is a pushing force that squashes or shortens a material (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how corrugated card is able to resist compression forces.
practice_questions.marks: Corrugated card has a wave-shaped (fluted) inner layer (1) sandwiched between two flat liner layers (1). The flutes act like a series of small arches (1) which distribute the compressive load and prevent the card from crushing flat (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why plywood is stronger than a single piece of timber of the same thickness. Refer to its structure in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Detailed explanation. Plywood is made from thin layers (veneers) glued together (1) with the grain direction alternating at 90° in each layer (1). Natural timber is strongest along the grain and weak across it (1). By alternating the grain, plywood resists forces in multiple directions (1), reducing the risk of splitting or warping (1). An odd number of layers ensures the board is balanced and stable (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic understanding of layers/grain.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of lamination as a method of reinforcing materials. Refer to at least two material categories in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation with examples from 2+ categories and a conclusion. Timber: plywood resists warping and multi-directional forces, but adds thickness and weight. Metals: laminated steel reduces eddy currents in transformer cores, but delamination can occur over time. Textiles: laminated fabrics (e.g. Gore-Tex) combine waterproofing with breathability, but can be expensive and hard to recycle. Polymers: laminated layers in packaging provide barrier properties. Conclusion on when lamination is most/least effective.
Mid band (4-6): Examples from at least one category with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Limited description, few or no examples.

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a lightweight shelving unit for a child’s bedroom. Discuss the forces the shelf will experience and how the designer could reinforce the structure to prevent failure.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion identifying specific forces (bending from weight on shelf, compression in uprights, shear at joints) with reinforcement solutions (gusset plates at corners, box-section uprights, laminated/manufactured board for shelves). Considers material choice (lightweight yet strong — e.g. plywood, aluminium). Links reinforcement to specific forces. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good identification of forces and some reinforcement methods.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Basic identification of forces with limited solutions.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial points, spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ecological footprint'.
practice_questions.marks: The total environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life, from raw material extraction to disposal (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a designer could reduce the product miles of a new table lamp.
practice_questions.marks: Source materials from local/UK suppliers to reduce transport distance (1). Manufacture the product in the same country where it will be sold (1). Also accept: use lightweight materials to reduce fuel consumption during transport.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the 'Repair' principle from the six Rs can reduce a product's environmental impact. Use an example.
practice_questions.marks: If a product can be repaired, it lasts longer (1) so fewer replacement products need to be manufactured, saving raw materials and energy (1). For example, Fairphone designs smartphones with replaceable modules (1) so a broken screen can be swapped without discarding the whole phone, reducing electronic waste (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the social issues a clothing manufacturer should consider when producing garments overseas.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Detailed explanation covering multiple issues. Safe working conditions — factories must meet health and safety standards, provide fire exits, and limit working hours (up to 2). Fair wages — workers should receive at least the minimum wage for their country and not be exploited (1). Pollution — textile dyeing can release harmful chemicals into rivers, affecting local communities (1). Child labour — some supply chains use underage workers, which is illegal and unethical (1). The Rana Plaza collapse (2013) shows the consequences of poor conditions (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited detail.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of recycling as a strategy for reducing a product's ecological footprint.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Benefits: diverts waste from landfill, conserves raw materials, recycled aluminium uses 95% less energy than virgin. Limitations: not all materials are easily recyclable (composites, mixed polymers), contamination reduces quality, recycling still requires energy and transport, downcycling means material quality degrades. Some materials (thermosetting polymers) cannot be recycled at all. Conclusion on effectiveness vs other strategies (reduce, re-use).
Mid band (4-6): Some benefits and limitations discussed.
Lower band (1-3): Basic description, one-sided argument.

practice_questions.text: A company wants to redesign its product packaging to be more sustainable. Discuss how the six Rs could be applied to reduce the packaging’s ecological and social footprint.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive application of all six Rs with specific packaging examples. Reduce: use thinner/lighter materials, smaller box sizes. Refuse: eliminate unnecessary layers like plastic windows. Re-use: design boxes customers can repurpose. Repair: not always applicable to packaging but reusable containers can be maintained. Recycle: switch to mono-materials (all cardboard) with clear recycling symbols. Rethink: could digital instructions replace printed inserts? Social: ensure cardboard from FSC sources, factory workers have safe conditions. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good application of 4–5 Rs with examples.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some Rs applied, limited examples.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial, spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'life cycle assessment'.
practice_questions.marks: A systematic method for evaluating the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life, from raw material extraction to disposal (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how crude oil is converted into a polymer such as polyethylene.
practice_questions.marks: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation to produce naphtha (1). The naphtha is cracked to produce monomers (ethene) which are then polymerised into polyethylene (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why seasoning is an important process in the production of timber-based products.
practice_questions.marks: Freshly cut (green) timber has a high moisture content (1). If used without seasoning, the timber will shrink as it dries, causing warping, splitting or cracking (1). Seasoning reduces the moisture content in a controlled way (1). This makes the timber dimensionally stable and suitable for use in furniture and construction (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the benefits and limitations of using a life cycle assessment when designing a new product.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Benefits: identifies which stage has the greatest environmental impact so the designer can focus improvements (1), helps compare materials objectively (1), supports marketing claims about sustainability (1). Limitations: LCA data can be complex and expensive to collect (1), results depend on assumptions (e.g. how long the product lasts) (1), does not always account for social factors (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic benefits or limitations only.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the environmental impact of using metals versus polymers as packaging materials. Consider their sources, processing and end-of-life disposal.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced comparison. Metals: mining ore is destructive and energy-intensive, especially aluminium (electrolysis). However, metals are infinitely recyclable with significant energy savings (aluminium: 95% less energy). Polymers: derived from crude oil (non-renewable), cheaper and lighter (reduces transport emissions), but most are not easily recycled and persist in the environment for centuries. Some polymers (PET) are recyclable but contamination limits rates. Conclusion on which is more sustainable and under what conditions.
Mid band (4-6): Covers both materials with some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Basic, one-sided description.

practice_questions.text: A company manufactures single-use paper coffee cups. Carry out a simplified life cycle assessment of this product, identifying the environmental impact at each stage and suggesting improvements.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive LCA covering all five stages. Extraction: trees felled (deforestation, habitat loss) — use FSC timber. Processing: pulping uses water and chemicals, plastic liner added (hard to separate for recycling) — use water-based coatings. Distribution: lightweight but high-volume transport — flat-pack and local manufacture. Use: single use means short lifespan — consider reusable alternatives. End of life: plastic liner prevents standard paper recycling, most go to landfill — switch to compostable liner. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good coverage of 3–4 stages with improvements.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some stages covered, limited improvements.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial. spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'stock forms'.
practice_questions.marks: The standard shapes and sizes in which materials are commercially available, such as sheets, rods, tubes and planks (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two stock forms in which metals are commercially available.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each correct stock form with brief description. E.g.: Sheet — flat pieces sold by length, width and thickness (1). Rod — solid cylindrical bar sold by length and diameter (1). Also accept: bar, tube, angle, channel.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a furniture manufacturer would use KD (knock-down) fittings in a flat-pack bookcase.
practice_questions.marks: KD fittings allow the product to be assembled by the customer at home (1), so it can be shipped flat-packed, reducing packaging size and transport costs (1). The fittings are designed to be assembled and disassembled, so the bookcase can be moved or reconfigured (1). Standard KD components (cam locks, barrel nuts) are cheap, widely available and do not require specialist tools (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of nesting when cutting components from a standard sheet of material. Refer to both cost and waste in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Nesting means arranging pattern pieces as closely together as possible (1) to minimise the amount of unused material (offcuts) (1). This reduces waste, which is better for the environment (1). It also saves money because fewer sheets need to be purchased (1). In mass production, even a small saving per unit multiplied by thousands of products adds up to a significant cost reduction (1). The kerf (width of the cut) should also be accounted for in the nesting layout (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic understanding of nesting with limited detail.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of standard components versus custom-made components in product manufacturing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Standard components: cheaper (mass-produced), readily available, consistent quality, easy to replace, simplify design. But: limited range of sizes/styles, may not fit a bespoke design, can make products look generic. Custom components: perfect fit for the design, unique aesthetics, can optimise performance. But: expensive to produce, longer lead times, harder to replace if broken. Conclusion on when each is most appropriate.
Mid band (4-6): Covers advantages and disadvantages of both with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): One-sided or superficial points.

practice_questions.text: A textile company is manufacturing 500 tote bags. Each bag requires a rectangle of fabric measuring 80 cm × 50 cm. The fabric is available in rolls 150 cm wide. Discuss how the company should plan the cutting layout to minimise waste, and calculate the minimum length of fabric needed.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Correct calculation with efficient layout. 150 cm width fits 1 bag (80 cm) plus another (80 cm would exceed 150 cm — OR could nest: 80+50=130 cm if rotated). Optimal: 3 pieces of 50 cm across the 150 cm width (3×50=150) with 80 cm length per row. That gives 3 bags per 80 cm. 500 ÷ 3 = 167 rows. 167 × 80 cm = 13,360 cm = 133.6 m minimum. Discussion of nesting strategy, seam allowances, fabric grain direction, pattern matching if printed, and kerf/cutting tolerance. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasonable calculation with some discussion of waste reduction.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Attempts calculation, limited discussion.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial or incorrect calculation. spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'batch production'.
practice_questions.marks: Manufacturing a set quantity of identical products before reconfiguring equipment for a different product (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between mass production and continuous production.
practice_questions.marks: Mass production makes large quantities on an assembly line but can be stopped and restarted (1). Continuous production runs 24/7 non-stop because halting the process would be impractical or damaging to equipment (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the unit cost of a product decreases as the scale of production increases.
practice_questions.marks: Higher production volumes allow the cost of tooling, machinery and setup to be spread across more units (1), reducing the cost per item (1). Bulk buying of materials reduces raw material costs (1). Automation replaces expensive skilled labour with faster, cheaper machine operations (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a small pottery studio producing handmade mugs would use a different scale of production to a company making disposable paper cups. Refer to specific scales in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): The pottery studio uses prototype/one-off production (1) because each mug is unique, made by hand on a potter’s wheel (1). The volume is low and customers pay a premium for the craftsmanship (1). The paper cup company uses continuous production (1) because demand is constant and high-volume, running 24/7 on automated machinery (1). Stopping the production line would waste materials and be expensive to restart (1).
Lower band (1-3): Names scales but limited explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether batch production or mass production would be more suitable for a company manufacturing school furniture. Consider cost, flexibility and product range.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Batch: allows different products (desks, chairs, shelving) to be made on the same equipment with retooling between runs; suits a range of sizes/styles; lower tooling investment. Mass: lower unit cost if demand is high enough; consistent quality; dedicated machinery. But: less flexible if the school wants custom sizes or finishes; high tooling cost only justified at very large volumes. Conclusion depends on order size and product variety.
Mid band (4-6): Covers both scales with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): One-sided or superficial.

practice_questions.text: A small electronics company has designed a new phone case. Initially they expect to sell 200 units per month, but if successful, demand could rise to 50,000 units per month. Discuss how their manufacturing scale and processes should change as demand grows.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion. Initial phase: batch production at 200/month using 3D printing or CNC machining — low tooling cost, quick to start, easy to modify design. Growth phase: investment in injection mould tooling as demand reaches thousands/month — high upfront cost but low per-unit cost, fast cycle times. At 50,000/month, full mass production with dedicated moulds, automated quality control, robotic assembly. Discusses transition points, financial risk, and how design may need to change for different processes (e.g. draft angles for injection moulding). spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion of at least two phases.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant points but limited progression.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial. spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'galvanising'.
practice_questions.marks: Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc to protect it from corrosion (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe one way a surface finish can improve the aesthetics of a timber product.
practice_questions.marks: Varnishing provides a transparent protective coat that enhances the natural grain and gives a warm appearance (1). It can also add a gloss or satin sheen that makes the surface look polished and professional (1). Accept: painting adds colour; staining enhances grain with colour.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a manufacturer would choose powder coating rather than painting for a set of outdoor metal garden chairs.
practice_questions.marks: Powder coating produces a thicker, more even finish than paint (1). It is more resistant to chipping, scratching and fading from UV exposure (1), so it lasts longer in outdoor conditions (1). The electrostatic application ensures full coverage including hard-to-reach areas, and the baked finish is tough and weather-resistant (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why tanalising is used on timber for outdoor garden products. Describe the process and its benefits.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Tanalising is a pressure treatment process (1). Timber is placed in a sealed chamber and chemical preservatives (e.g. copper-based compounds) are forced deep into the wood under pressure (1). This protects the timber against rot, fungal decay and insect attack (1). It extends the lifespan of outdoor products like fencing, decking and garden furniture significantly (1). The chemicals penetrate deep into the wood rather than just coating the surface, so even if the surface is scratched or cut, the interior is still protected (1). The greenish tint can fade over time, and the timber can still be painted or stained on top (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic description of the process or benefits.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of dip coating versus galvanising as a surface treatment for a steel bike rack that will be installed outdoors.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Dip coating: provides a colourful, smooth polymer coating that resists corrosion and adds aesthetic appeal; soft coating absorbs minor impacts without chipping; but can be damaged by sharp scratches, exposing the steel beneath. Galvanising: zinc layer provides excellent long-term corrosion protection even if scratched (sacrificial protection); very durable; but limited colour options (silver/grey), rougher texture, less visually appealing. Both are suitable for outdoor use. Conclusion based on whether aesthetics or raw durability is the priority.
Mid band (4-6): Covers both finishes with some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Describes one or both finishes with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: A company is manufacturing a range of kitchen utensils (spatulas, spoons, tongs) from stainless steel with polymer handles. Discuss the surface treatments and finishes that should be applied to both the metal and polymer parts. Consider functional and aesthetic requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion. Metal parts: stainless steel already has corrosion resistance but may be polished to a mirror or brushed finish for aesthetics and hygiene (easy to clean). Food-safe requirement — no toxic coatings. Polymer handles: must be food-safe, heat-resistant, comfortable grip. Soft-touch overmoulding or textured finish for grip; colour through the polymer (pigmented granules) rather than surface paint which could chip into food. Dip coating could add colour but must be food-grade. Discusses: food safety regulations, dishwasher resistance, heat tolerance near cooking surfaces, brand identity through colour. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion covering both materials.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Covers one material well, other briefly.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial. spelling/grammar errors.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the purpose of seasoning timber?
A) To add preservative chemicals under pressure
B) To reduce the moisture content of freshly felled wood
C) To harden the surface of the timber using heat
D) To apply a decorative stain to the grain
Describe one way in which the properties of paper or board are modified to make it suitable for food packaging.
practice_questions.marks: A thin polyethylene laminate layer is applied to the inner surface of the board (1), which prevents moisture from soaking through and weakening the structure (1). Accept: wax coating / clay-based barrier treatment with explanation of how it prevents moisture transfer.

practice_questions.text: Explain why polypropylene is a suitable material for school and office seating. Refer to at least two of its properties.
practice_questions.marks: Polypropylene has high impact resistance so it withstands everyday knocks and heavy use without cracking (1). It is lightweight, making chairs easy to move and stack (1). It can be injection-moulded into ergonomic shapes in a single process, reducing manufacturing cost (1). It is available in a wide range of colours, removing the need for painting (1). Max 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain what annealing is, why it is carried out on metals, and describe an example of where it is used in commercial manufacturing.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Annealing is a heat treatment in which a metal is heated to a specific temperature and then allowed to cool slowly (1). It relieves internal stresses caused by cold-working processes such as rolling or pressing (1), restoring the metal's softness and malleability so that further forming can be carried out without cracking (1). Example: copper pipe is annealed so it can be bent to shape without splitting during installation (1). Steel sheet is annealed between rolling passes to allow it to be reduced to thin gauges in commercial strip production (1). Without annealing, work-hardened metal would crack if further deformation is attempted (1).
Lower band (1-3): Partial description of annealing or limited link to commercial use.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the suitability of aluminium and stainless steel as materials for a commercial frying pan, with reference to their physical and mechanical properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Aluminium: very high thermal conductivity — heats quickly and evenly (1); low density — pan is lightweight (1); malleable — deep-drawn into pan shape efficiently (1); however softer surface scratches more easily and may react with acidic foods unless anodised (1). Stainless steel: excellent corrosion resistance and food safety (1); harder surface resists scratching (1); lower thermal conductivity so may have hot spots unless an aluminium core is added (1); heavier than aluminium (1). Conclusion: aluminium suits budget / everyday cooking where weight matters; stainless steel suits professional or long-life products where durability and hygiene are priorities (1). Evidence of weighing both sides required for top band.
Mid band (4-6): Covers both materials with some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Describes one material with little comparison.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is designing a range of outdoor garden furniture using three different materials: timber, mild steel and high-density polyethylene (HDPE). Discuss how the properties of each material affect its performance in an outdoor environment, and explain what modifications or treatments are needed to ensure long-term durability.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion of all three materials. Timber: susceptible to moisture absorption (warping, rot, splitting) — seasoning removes excess moisture before use; tanalising or oil treatment needed to protect in service; grain and natural appearance are aesthetic advantages but need maintenance. Mild steel: strong and formable but rusts rapidly outdoors — galvanising (zinc coating), powder coating or paint required; powder coating also improves aesthetics; uncoated steel has limited outdoor lifespan. HDPE: inherently weather-resistant, UV-stable (especially with UV stabiliser additives), will not rot or corrode, minimal maintenance; lower strength than steel but sufficient for seating; less visually premium than timber. Conclusion considers maintenance, cost of modification, lifecycle and aesthetics. Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar throughout.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion of all three with some treatment detail.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Two materials discussed, limited treatment detail.
Lower band (1-3): One material or superficial points.

before.description: How properties of materials are exploited and modified in commercial products across all six material categories.
before.content_html:
Properties in Action

Every commercial product relies on the physical and mechanical properties of its materials to function reliably. Physical properties — density, thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity — determine how a material behaves in its environment. Mechanical properties — strength, hardness, toughness, elasticity — determine whether it can withstand the forces placed on it during use. In the exam, questions ask you to link specific properties to specific products and explain why those properties matter.

Key Fact

The six material categories in AQA D&T are: papers & boards, timber, metals, polymers, textiles, and electronic & mechanical systems. Each category has distinct properties that make it suitable for specific commercial products.

Papers & Boards

Workability is the defining property of papers and boards. Corrugated cardboard is lightweight yet has excellent compressive strength, protecting goods during transit. Folding boxboard used for card food packaging has a smooth, printable surface combined with enough stiffness to hold its shape on a supermarket shelf. A cereal box, for example, must be rigid enough to stack, printable for branding, and low-cost for mass production — folding boxboard meets all three requirements. However, papers and boards absorb moisture and lose strength when wet, which limits their use in damp or food-contact environments without modification.

Timber

Timber's high strength-to-weight ratio and ease of machining make it ideal for flat-pack furniture. Components such as shelving panels are cut to precise dimensions, sanded smooth, and joined using cam-lock fittings — a system that is only possible because timber-based boards like MDF and chipboard are dimensionally stable and accept screws reliably. Solid hardwoods such as oak are used for tabletops where surface hardness is needed to resist scratching. The natural moisture content of timber varies, which can cause warping and splitting unless the material is properly conditioned before use.

Metals

Metals combine high strength, thermal conductivity and formability, making them the material of choice for cooking utensils such as pots, pans and baking trays. Stainless steel's resistance to corrosion and its non-reactive surface make it food-safe; aluminium's high thermal conductivity and low density allow a pan to heat quickly while remaining lightweight. Malleability allows metals to be pressed or rolled into complex shapes — deep-drawn stainless steel sinks and aluminium cooking pots are formed this way in commercial manufacturing.

Stainless steel: corrosion resistance + hygiene → cutlery, cookware, surgical instruments.

Aluminium: lightweight + thermal conductivity + formability → pans, drink cans, foil packaging.

Copper: excellent electrical conductivity + ductility → electrical wiring, plumbing pipes.

Mild steel: strength + weldability + low cost → car body panels, structural frameworks, shelving.

Polymers

Polymers are mouldable, lightweight, electrically insulating, and available in a huge range of colours — which is why injection-moulded polypropylene seating is standard in schools and offices. Polypropylene has sufficient impact resistance to survive everyday use, enough flexibility to hinge (the 'living hinge' is a classic polypropylene design feature), and a surface that can be moulded in any colour without painting. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) is used for outdoor polymer seating and playground equipment because it combines UV resistance with toughness and will not rust, rot or splinter.

Textiles

Sportswear demands textiles that combine strength, elasticity, moisture management and light weight. Lycra (elastane) blended with polyester gives compression sportswear its stretch and recovery. Nylon's high tensile strength and abrasion resistance make it ideal for sports shoe uppers and kit bags. Performance fabrics such as Gore-Tex exploit expanded PTFE membranes to be simultaneously waterproof and breathable — a critical property combination for outdoor sports clothing. In contrast, cotton and linen are used in casual sportswear where comfort and breathability matter more than elasticity or water resistance.

Electronic & Mechanical Systems

Domestic appliances combine materials from multiple categories, but their electronic and mechanical systems have their own material requirements. Copper's electrical conductivity makes it the standard conductor in wiring and PCB tracks. Steel and engineering polymers such as nylon and acetal are used in gears, bearings and structural brackets within appliances because they combine strength with low friction. Housings for electronics must be electrically insulating, lightweight and capable of being moulded to complex ergonomic shapes — ABS polymer is the default for appliance casings, remote controls and tool housings.

Key Fact

When selecting a material for a commercial product, designers must match the material's properties to the forces, environments and use conditions the product will face — not just choose the cheapest or most familiar option.

Modifying Properties — Papers & Boards

Raw paper absorbs moisture readily — a serious problem for food packaging. Additives to prevent moisture transfer, such as wax coatings, polyethylene laminate layers or clay-coated barrier treatments, are incorporated into food-grade board. A milk carton or juice box is made from folding boxboard laminated with a thin layer of polyethylene on the inside surface — the board provides structural rigidity while the polyethylene prevents liquid from soaking through. This modification allows a paper-based material to perform in a wet food environment where unmodified board would collapse within minutes.

Modifying Properties — Timber

Freshly felled ('green') timber contains a high moisture content — up to 100% in some species — which causes it to shrink, warp and crack as it dries. Seasoning removes this excess moisture in a controlled way. Air seasoning stacks timber in open sheds for months or years; kiln seasoning uses heated chambers to reduce moisture content in days. Properly seasoned timber is dimensionally stable and far less likely to split or distort in service — an essential property for flat-pack furniture joints and high-quality joinery.

Modifying Properties — Metals

Some metalworking processes cause metals to become hardened and brittle through work-hardening — repeated cold forming introduces internal stresses that make the metal crack if further forming is attempted. Annealing reverses this by heating the metal to a set temperature and allowing it to cool slowly. This restores the metal's softness and malleability, making further forming possible. Copper pipe is annealed to allow it to be bent without splitting; steel sheet is annealed between rolling passes to allow it to be reduced to thin gauges.

Polymers — UV stabilisers: Many polymers, particularly polypropylene and polyethylene, degrade when exposed to ultraviolet radiation — they become brittle, discolour and eventually crack. UV stabiliser additives (e.g. hindered amine light stabilisers, HALS) are compounded into the polymer during manufacture, absorbing or scattering UV energy before it can break polymer chains. Garden furniture, agricultural films and outdoor signage all rely on UV-stabilised polymers to resist degradation over years of sun exposure.

Textiles — flame retardants: Untreated natural fibres such as cotton and wool will ignite and sustain combustion. Flame retardant treatments — chemical compounds such as phosphorus-based agents applied during finishing — interrupt the combustion process by inhibiting the release of flammable gases. This modification is legally required for upholstered furniture fabrics in the UK under the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire Safety) Regulations. Children's nightwear and contract furnishing fabrics must meet strict flame-spread standards.

Electronic & mechanical — photosensitive PCB board and anodising: Standard fibreglass PCB board is coated with a photosensitive layer to allow circuit tracks to be printed photographically — UV light hardens the resist coating where tracks are required. The unhardened resist is washed away in a developer solution, exposing the copper beneath those areas. Acid (ferric chloride) then etches away the exposed copper, leaving only the protected copper tracks under the hardened resist. Aluminium components in mechanical and electronic enclosures are often anodised: an electrochemical process that grows a hard aluminium oxide layer on the surface, dramatically increasing hardness and wear resistance. Anodised aluminium is used on laptop casings, camera bodies and heatsinks.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of an addition process?
A) Die cutting
B) Turning on a lathe
C) Vacuum forming
D) Welding
Describe the purpose of using a jig in a manufacturing workshop.
practice_questions.marks: A jig holds the workpiece in a fixed, accurate position (1) and guides the cutting or drilling tool so that identical results are produced on every component in the batch (1). Accept: ensures repeatability / reduces the skill required from the operator.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by manufacturing to a tolerance. Give an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Tolerance is the acceptable range of variation in a dimension (1), defined by an upper limit and a lower limit (1). A component is accepted if its measurement falls within these limits and rejected if it falls outside them (1). Example: a metal shaft with a nominal diameter of 20 mm and a tolerance of ±0.1 mm is acceptable between 19.9 mm and 20.1 mm — this ensures it fits the mating bearing correctly (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the vacuum forming process and explain why it is used commercially for food packaging trays.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): A thermoplastic sheet (e.g. PET or HIPS) is clamped in a frame and heated until it softens (1). The softened sheet is lowered over a mould (1). Air is evacuated beneath the sheet so atmospheric pressure forces the sheet tightly against the mould's surface (1). The sheet cools and hardens in the mould's shape, then is trimmed to the final product (1). It is used for food trays because it is fast, low tooling cost and can produce complex shapes in thin-gauge plastic efficiently (1). The mould can be reproduced identically thousands of times per hour, making it cost-effective for mass production (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic description of heating and moulding without detail of the pressure mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Compare die cutting with CNC routing as commercial wastage processes for producing flat timber components. Consider accuracy, production rate and suitability.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Die cutting: used mainly for thin sheet materials (paper, board, thin textiles); a shaped steel rule die cuts, creases and perforates in a single press stroke; very high production rate (millions per hour); low cost per part for large volumes; limited to thin, flat materials; tooling cost of die is high upfront. CNC routing: cuts timber sheet or solid wood along computer-programmed paths; excellent accuracy (±0.1 mm); can produce complex 2D and some 3D profiles; suitable for furniture panels, architectural joinery, signage; slower cycle time than die cutting; no need for bespoke tooling (tool path changed in software); better for smaller batches or varied profiles. Die cutting suits mass production of identical flat shapes; CNC routing suits varied, higher-value components. Comparison of both sides required for top band.
Mid band (4-6): Some comparison with one process described well.
Lower band (1-3): Mostly descriptive, little comparison.

practice_questions.text: Accept as LOW severity simplification if the spec only requires 'blow moulding' for GCSE, but update the mark scheme to note that PET bottles specifically use injection stretch blow moulding where a preform is heated, stretched and blown rather than an extruded parison. Explain both processes and discuss why each is more suitable for its product than the other would be.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Injection moulding: molten polymer is forced under high pressure into a precision steel mould cavity; the polymer cools and the mould opens to eject the part; produces complex, high-detail parts with tight tolerances; very fast cycle time; high tooling cost offset by large volumes; ideal for solid, small, complex parts like bottle caps — the thread, tamper-evident band and sealing ring need dimensional precision. Blow moulding: a hot polymer parison (tube) is clamped in a split mould and compressed air inflates it to fill the mould cavity; used for hollow thin-walled containers; produces lightweight, seamless, hollow forms; PET bottles need thin walls and uniform thickness — achievable by blow moulding, not by injection moulding (which would require enormous material volume for a hollow bottle). Discussion of why each process suits its product and not the other's: injection moulding cannot produce a thin-walled hollow bottle efficiently; blow moulding cannot achieve the fine surface detail and thread precision of a bottle cap. Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar throughout.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Both processes described well with reasonable comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-6): One process described in detail, other briefly.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial or confused description of processes.

before.content_html:
Production Aids

Before any material is cut or shaped, designers and manufacturers set up datum points and use production aids to ensure accuracy and repeatability. Working to a datum means all measurements are taken from a single fixed reference point or edge — this prevents the accumulation of small errors that would occur if each measurement were taken from the last cut. Templates allow a shape to be reproduced identically on multiple workpieces: a plywood template for a curved guitar body, or a card net template for a packaging blank. Jigs hold the workpiece and guide the tool — a drilling jig ensures holes are made in exactly the same position on every component in a batch, which is essential for interchangeable parts.

Key Fact

Production aids — templates, jigs and patterns — improve accuracy, repeatability and speed in both workshop and commercial manufacturing. They also reduce the skill level required, allowing less experienced operators to produce consistent results.

Calculating Material Quantities

Before manufacturing begins, a designer must calculate how much material is needed to avoid waste and control costs. For sheet materials, this involves calculating the material yield — how many components can be cut from a standard sheet with minimal offcuts. Nesting shapes closely together on a sheet, or arranging pattern pieces on fabric to follow the grain efficiently, maximises yield. In commercial production, computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) software automates this nesting process. For timber, the volume needed is calculated from finished dimensions plus allowances for sawing, planing and shrinkage during seasoning.

Wastage Processes

Wastage processes start with a block or sheet and remove material until the finished shape is achieved. In commercial paper and board production, die cutting uses a shaped steel blade pressed into the board to cut out net shapes for boxes and packaging in a single action — millions of identical cartons are die-cut each hour in automated lines. Perforation creates rows of small holes to allow controlled tearing, used on tear-off strips in packaging and stationery. For metals and timber, sawing (circular saw, bandsaw) removes material along straight or curved lines; drilling removes cylindrical cores; milling uses rotating cutters to remove material from flat or profiled surfaces; turning on a lathe removes material from a spinning workpiece to produce cylindrical or tapered forms. Cutting and shearing — guillotine cutting for sheet metal, rotary cutting for fabric — remove material along a straight line rapidly and with little waste.

Papers & boards: Die cutting is the dominant commercial process. A shaped steel rule die is mounted in a press; each stroke cuts, creases and perforates the board blank in one pass. Offset lithography is often combined on the same line, printing before cutting.

Timber: CNC routing removes material from sheet timber or solid wood along computer-programmed paths. It is used for furniture components, architectural joinery and signage, and can produce identical complex shapes repeatedly without manual setting-out.

Metals: CNC milling and turning are standard in engineering production. Laser cutting and plasma cutting use high-energy beams to cut thin sheet metal with minimal heat distortion and very fine tolerances.

Textiles: Automated knife cutting or die cutting lays multiple plies of fabric on a table and cuts through all layers simultaneously, reducing labour and waste.

Addition Processes

Addition processes join materials or build up shapes. Welding melts and fuses metal parts together — MIG welding is the standard commercial process for steel structures, car bodies and metal furniture frames. Brazing joins metals using a filler alloy at a lower temperature than welding, preserving the base metal's properties — used for copper pipework and cycle frames. Soldering uses a low-temperature tin-based alloy to make electrical connections on PCBs; the solder flows into the joint and hardens on cooling. Lamination bonds layers of material together to create a composite with improved properties — laminated safety glass, plywood, and foam-backed textiles are all examples. 3D printing is an addition process — fused deposition modelling (FDM) deposits thermoplastic filament layer by layer to build complex forms impossible to achieve by conventional machining. Batik uses wax applied to fabric to resist dye, adding pattern. Sewing joins fabric panels using interlocking thread stitches — the fundamental process in garment assembly. Bonding uses adhesives (e.g. epoxy resin, contact adhesive, acrylic cement) to join materials without heat. Printing adds ink to surfaces — screen printing, digital printing and pad printing each suit different substrates and batch sizes.

Key Fact

The three families of shaping and fabricating processes are: wastage (material is removed), addition (material is joined or deposited) and deforming & reforming (material is reshaped without removing or adding it). AQA questions often ask which family a named process belongs to.

Deforming & Reforming Processes

Deforming and reforming processes change shape without losing material. For polymers, vacuum forming heats a thermoplastic sheet until it softens, clamps it over a mould, then evacuates the air beneath so atmospheric pressure forces the sheet to conform to the mould's shape — used commercially for blister packs, trays and chocolate box inserts. Blow moulding forces compressed air into a hot polymer parison (tube) inside a split mould, inflating it to the mould's shape — the standard process for HDPE containers such as milk and shampoo bottles. PET drinks bottles instead use injection stretch blow moulding, where an injection-moulded preform is reheated, stretched with a rod and blown to shape. Injection moulding forces molten polymer under high pressure into a precision steel mould cavity — it produces complex, high-detail parts in seconds and is used for everything from bottle caps to car dashboard components. Extrusion pushes molten polymer through a shaped die to produce continuous profiles — guttering, window frames and plastic pipes are all extruded. For metals, pressing (e.g. deep drawing) forces sheet metal into a die to produce hollow forms such as cans and sinks; casting pours molten metal into a mould and allows it to solidify. For papers and boards, creasing uses a blunt rule to compress the board along a line so it folds cleanly without cracking — essential for packaging nets. For textiles, drape forming heats thermoplastic-coated fabric over a mould to produce shaped components for upholstery and protective equipment. Bending and folding apply to both sheet metal and thermoplastic sheet — a press brake bends metal along a straight line; a strip heater softens acrylic along a narrow zone so it can be bent by hand.

Manufacturing to a Tolerance

In commercial production, no two components will ever be absolutely identical — slight variations are unavoidable. Tolerance defines the acceptable range of variation: a component with a nominal diameter of 20 mm and a tolerance of ±0.5 mm is acceptable anywhere between 19.5 mm and 20.5 mm. Tolerances must be tight enough to ensure parts fit together and function correctly, but not so tight that they become expensive to achieve. Measuring instruments such as micrometers and vernier callipers are used to check whether components fall within tolerance. Components outside the tolerance range are rejected at the quality control stage — a process called inspection.

Metals: Engineering components such as bearing housings and threaded fasteners are manufactured to very tight tolerances (±0.01 mm or tighter) to ensure interchangeability. On a car assembly line, every bolt must fit every matching nut without individual selection.

Timber: Tolerances are wider (±1 mm is common for joinery) because wood is a natural material that expands and contracts with humidity. Door and window frames include intentional clearance gaps to allow for seasonal movement.

Textiles: Seam allowances define the tolerance for garment construction — typically 10–15 mm. Pattern pieces include this allowance so the finished garment meets its design dimensions.

Papers & boards: Die-cut packaging blanks are held to tight dimensional tolerances (±0.5 mm) to ensure panels fold and lock together correctly on automated assembly lines.
before.description: Production aids, shaping processes, tolerances and commercial manufacturing methods in design and technology.
